description: We are a multidisciplinary team of Senegalese students passionate about science, technology, and space. We are pooling our skills to develop an innovative solution for monitoring the health of astronauts. Our team values ​​creativity, curiosity, collaboration, and team spirit.
summary: SpaceBio is a health-monitoring prototype for astronaut crews on long-duration missions. Crew members and flight doctors follow vital signs, bone health, sleep and anomalies through a single app that supports two modes, Space Mode and Earth Mode for post-flight reconditioning. The problem is that crews face bone loss, cardiovascular and sleep changes, and communication delays of about 18 minutes that limit real-time medical support. SpaceBio responds with personalized baselines: each indicator is compared with the crew member’s own rolling 14-day reference, and deviations above two standard deviations are flagged for an expert to validate. An interactive body map links each organ system to its measures, a bone-risk model estimates risk without replacing DXA scans, and asynchronous messaging connects astronauts with their doctors. Consent is recorded for each data use, and the interface is available in 11 languages. All data is simulated, and the tool supports evaluation, not diagnosis. It matters because early, personalized detection of drift lets teams act sooner, and it helps crews return to Earth more safely.
details:
SpaceBio is a health-monitoring prototype for crews on long-duration space missions. The astronaut tracks their vital signs, bone load and countdown to return, while the flight doctor reviews patients in read-only mode, sorted by alert severity.

How it works: each user chooses their role (astronaut, flight doctor or network administrator), their language (11 languages) and their mode (Space or Earth). The dashboard shows the mission, vital signs with a 7-day trend and the brain follow-up. The body map displays a simulated 3D silhouette with brain, lungs, heart and skeleton. Clicking an organ opens its metrics, a trace and a recommendation. Each measurement is compared with the person’s own rolling 14-day baseline, and deviations above two standard deviations are flagged with a suggested action to be validated by an expert. Measurements can be entered manually or taken contactlessly through camera and microphone, with consent. The astronaut–doctor messaging shows the relay delay (about 18 to 25 minutes) and lets users attach a telemetry trend. An administrator area presents, in anonymized form, the partner sites, anomalies by cohort and model performance by subgroup.

Benefits: signals take several minutes to reach Earth. A single view of trends, ranked alerts and reports helps the crew and the doctor act earlier, without waiting for a real-time reply. Guest mode lets people explore the tool without an account or registration.

Expected impact: shorten the time needed to detect a physiological drift, better prioritize medical time, and prepare the return (bone-load tracking, end-of-mission reports). The anonymized learning network, launched only with explicit consent, aims to compare results across sites and profiles (female and male crews aged 28 to 45, flights longer than 30 days, analogue isolation). SpaceBio is not a diagnostic tool and has not been clinically validated: it is a prototype.

Tools and software: Google AI Studio for the web app, Lovable, SVG for the silhouette and traces, Google Fonts (Orbitron, Inter, JetBrains Mono). AI assistants used for code and text: Claude (Anthropic) and Google AI Studio. No specific hardware: the prototype runs in a web browser.

Creativity: holographic silhouette whose heartbeat, breathing and blood flow follow the simulated data; four mission scenarios (Nominal, Spacewalk, Bone Alert, Solar Storm) that change rhythms and colors; a dark, sober interface designed for calm use during a mission.

Factors considered: crew safety and the absence of automatic diagnosis; communication delays with Earth; privacy (separate consents, export and deletion of local data); inclusion (11 languages, adjustable text size); diversity of profiles (indicators by subgroup); transparency (simulated data labelled throughout, NASA image credits in the footer).

All data shown is simulated and labelled “Simulated data.”

Title: SpaceBio: Test Scenario and Visual Evidence

Scenario A: Healthy astronaut (baseline)
This test checks the healthy case. The baseline is loaded, and every indicator should read Nominal, with no active alert and no deviation from the crew member’s 14-day reference.

  • Dashboard with all vital signs in the Nominal range (heart rate 62 bpm, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg).
  • Settings page after loading the healthy baseline. The confirmation message shows that all indicators are Nominal and that no alert is active.
  • Alerts page with no active alert. The log records the loaded healthy baseline as its first event.

Anomaly page showing no deviation above 2 standard deviations over the 14-day rolling window, compared with the crew member’s own baseline.

Scenario B: Sleep deterioration
The sleep anomaly scenario is loaded, showing three nights averaging 5.9 h. A manual entry of 5.9 h is then recorded. The test checks that the sleep alert is raised, delivered to the on-duty flight doctor, and shown on the dashboard. The alert is created when the scenario is loaded; the manual entry confirms the value.

  • Settings page after loading the sleep anomaly scenario. The message shows a 3-night average of 5.9 h and that the alert was created and routed to the on-duty doctor.
  • Manual entry of sleep duration: 5.9 h recorded for day 31. The history shows the entry with the status Surveillance (monitoring).
  • Alert “cumulative sleep duration below target”: 3-night average of 5.9 h against a 6.5–9.0 h window, with the threshold “Moy. 3 j < 6,2 h”. The notification is marked Remise (delivered) to the on-duty flight doctor.
  • Bottom of the dashboard, showing the onboard alert and notification status. The sleep alert appears with the status.

Scenario C: Link loss and store-and-forward
The link with Earth is cut. A heart-rate measurement of 70 bpm is entered before and after saving, to show that it is kept on board in the queue. The test checks that the active alert stays visible during the loss, and that once the link is restored, the queued data is sent once, in order, with no duplicate.

Settings page after simulating a link loss. The red banner shows that data is kept on board, and the queue is empty (0).

  • Heart rate entry (70 bpm) ready but not yet saved. The link is lost and the queue is empty, so the measure has not been sent.
  • After saving, the 70 bpm measure is placed in the queue (1 item). The message confirms that it stays on board until the link returns.
  • The sleep alert stays visible while the link is lost. The top bar shows lost, and the banner shows 1 item in the queue.
  • Sync log after the link is restored. The queued measure was sent once, in order, with no duplicate. The first four rows show the restoration, the measure, the queued entry and the link loss.

Scenario D: Acknowledgement
The flight doctor acknowledges the notification. The test checks that its status changes to Acknowledged, and that the astronaut sees the same status.

  • Flight doctor view: the notification is now marked acknowledged. Acknowledgement is the only write action allowed to the doctor in this view.
  • Astronaut view: the same alert shows acknowledged, so the crew member can see that the doctor has taken it into account.

Scenario E: Escalation
Nobody acknowledges the alert. After 30 simulated minutes, it is escalated to the backup doctor, Dr Claire Moreau. The red line and the escalation log show this. Known limit: the recipient field still shows the on-duty doctor.

  • Settings page after advancing the simulated time by 30 minutes. The time moves from 06:17PM to 06:47PM, which triggers the escalation rule.
  • Astronaut view: the alert is marked escalated. The red line names the backup doctor, Dr. Claire Moreau, after 30 simulated minutes without acknowledgement. The recipient field still shows the on-duty doctor, which is a known limit of the prototype.
  • Flight doctor view: the same notification is marked escalated and remains open for acknowledgement.
